# Hidden expert knowledge: identifying common minerals in hand sample

Persona: Dr. Sam Okafor, field geologist, 20 years teaching undergraduate field mapping. Talks fast, uses jargon, assumes a lot. Says "you just get a feel for it" when tired of explaining.

## Facts (numbered; used for the capture score)
1. The goal is to name the mineral confidently using only a hand lens, a steel knife, a glass plate, a streak plate, a magnet and dilute HCl — no lab.
2. Doing it well means you can justify the ID from at least three independent properties, not one.
3. Always start with a fresh surface; weathered surfaces lie about colour and lustre. Knock or scratch off the rind.
4. Order of tests: lustre first, then hardness, then streak, then cleavage/fracture, then habit, then special tests (acid, magnetism, taste, heft).
5. Colour is the least reliable property; many minerals come in many colours (quartz can be clear, white, pink, purple, smoky).
6. Lustre: first decide metallic vs non-metallic — does it look like polished metal and is it opaque even at thin edges?
7. Non-metallic lustres to distinguish: vitreous (glassy, like quartz), pearly (like the cleavage face of mica or talc), silky (fibrous, like satin spar gypsum), earthy/dull (like kaolinite).
8. Hardness uses the Mohs scale, 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
9. Fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin about 3.5, a steel knife blade about 5.5, glass about 5.5, a steel file about 6.5.
10. To test hardness, try to scratch the sample with the knife, pressing firmly; then try to scratch the glass plate with the sample.
11. Common beginner error: mistaking a powder trail (the softer material rubbing off) for a scratch. Wipe it with your thumb — a real scratch is a groove that stays; a powder line wipes away.
12. Test hardness on a small, inconspicuous spot and on a single crystal, not on a crumbly aggregate, because aggregates break apart and seem softer than they are.
13. Streak is the colour of the mineral's powder, made by dragging it across the unglazed back of a porcelain tile.
14. Streak is most useful for metallic minerals; most non-metallic minerals have a white or colourless streak.
15. Minerals harder than the streak plate (about 6.5–7), like quartz, won't leave a streak — they scratch the plate instead.
16. Hematite can look black, silver or red but always has a red-brown ("cherry/ketchup") streak.
17. Cleavage: the mineral breaks along flat, repeating planes that reflect light all together as you rotate it under a light — look for a "flash".
18. Fracture: an irregular or curved break with no flat planes; conchoidal fracture (shell-like curved ridges, like broken glass) is diagnostic of quartz.
19. Count cleavage directions and their angles: mica has one perfect cleavage (peels into sheets); feldspar has two at about 90°; calcite has three not at 90° (rhombohedral); halite three at 90° (cubes).
20. Beginners confuse crystal faces with cleavage planes. Crystal faces are on the outside of a grown crystal; cleavage planes repeat inside as parallel steps when you break it.
21. Habit is the characteristic shape: cubic (pyrite, halite, galena), prismatic hexagonal columns with pointed terminations (quartz), bladed, fibrous, platy (mica), botryoidal (bubbly, like some hematite).
22. Calcite fizzes vigorously in cold dilute (about 10%) HCl. Dolomite fizzes only weakly, or only when powdered (scratch it first and put acid on the powder).
23. Acid safety: use dropper bottle, a single drop, goggles, rinse the sample and your hands; never put acid on a sample someone else wants to keep pristine.
24. Quartz vs calcite (the classic confusion): both can be white/clear and glassy. Quartz scratches glass, has no cleavage (conchoidal fracture), doesn't fizz. Calcite is scratched by a knife (hardness 3), has three rhombic cleavages and fizzes.
25. Clear calcite shows double refraction: a line viewed through a rhomb appears doubled.
26. Pyrite vs chalcopyrite vs gold: pyrite is pale brassy yellow, hard (6–6.5, scratches glass, can't be scratched by a knife), greenish-black streak, often cubic with striations on faces.
27. Chalcopyrite is a deeper brassy yellow, often with an iridescent blue/purple tarnish, softer (3.5–4, the knife scratches it), greenish-black streak.
28. Gold is soft (2.5–3), malleable (it dents and doesn't shatter under a needle), has a golden-yellow streak and is extremely heavy for its size.
29. "Fool's gold" test in one move: press a pin point into it. Gold dents; pyrite won't scratch; chalcopyrite scratches and powders.
30. Heft (specific gravity by feel): bounce the sample in your palm and compare to a similar-sized piece of quartz. Galena, gold and barite feel surprisingly heavy.
31. Galena: metallic silver-grey, perfect cubic cleavage (breaks into cubes), lead-grey streak, very heavy, soft (2.5).
32. Magnetite is strongly magnetic (attracts a magnet or a compass needle), black, black streak, hardness about 6.
33. Halite tastes salty and has cubic cleavage; only lick a sample if you know it's not something toxic, and never in a shared collection.
34. Muscovite (clear/silvery) and biotite (black/dark brown) are micas: peel into thin, flexible elastic sheets with a fingernail.
35. Orthoclase (K-feldspar) is often pink/salmon; plagioclase is white-grey and shows fine parallel striations (lines) on cleavage faces — tilt it in the light to see them.
36. Gypsum is softer than a fingernail (2) — your nail scratches it; calcite is not scratched by a fingernail. This is the quick gypsum vs calcite check.
37. Edge case: very fine-grained or massive samples (no visible crystals) — cleavage and habit become useless; rely on hardness, streak, lustre, acid, and heft, and be less confident.
38. Edge case: a coating or tarnish (e.g. iron-oxide staining, chalcopyrite tarnish) can make lustre and colour misleading — always test a fresh broken surface.
39. Edge case: rocks are mixtures of minerals; make sure each test is on one grain of one mineral, using the hand lens to check you're on a single grain.
40. Quality check: write down each property you observed, then check your ID against a determinative table; if two properties disagree with the table, your ID is wrong or you tested the wrong grain — re-test.
41. Quality check: ask "what else could it be?" and name the one property that rules out each lookalike.
42. Beginners over-trust colour and under-use hardness; the knife and glass plate are the most powerful tools in the kit.
